text: Solving the Schrödinger equation for a simple two-level system — exactly the kind of system a qubit is — produces a specific, concrete matrix: the time-evolution operator U of t. This lesson works through a fully verified example of what that matrix looks like and what it does.

Take the Hamiltonian H equal to h-bar omega over 2, times the Pauli-Z matrix. The solution is U of t equals the exponential of negative i H t over h-bar, which works out to a diagonal matrix with entries e to the negative i omega t over 2, and e to the positive i omega t over 2. Both diagonal entries have magnitude exactly 1 for any value of t — verified directly — which is exactly the condition for U of t to be unitary.

Plug in a specific moment, theta equals omega-t-over-2 equals pi over 4. Applying U of t to ket-zero just multiplies it by an overall phase factor — since ket-zero has nothing to compare that phase against, this has zero observable effect; P of 0 stays 1. But applying the exact same U of t to ket-plus gives components 0.5 minus 0.5i and 0.5 plus 0.5i — the probabilities stay 0.5 and 0.5, unchanged, but factoring out the common phase leaves a genuine relative phase of i between the two terms. That relative phase is real and physical, even though neither probability changed.

A matrix U is unitary if U-dagger U equals the identity — its conjugate transpose times itself. That condition is exactly what guarantees the inner product of the state with itself stays equal to 1 for all time: if the state started normalized, it stays normalized forever. Every gate in a real quantum circuit is unitary for exactly this reason — it has to represent some valid stretch of Schrödinger-equation evolution, and probability conservation forces unitarity.
Next lesson shows that the Hamiltonian, the generator of time evolution, is simultaneously the energy observable — and works through exactly what that means with the same verified Hamiltonian.
